evidence.note: Chose SQLite as durable seq authority with a killable broadcaster + DB-polling fallback — an inherently broadcaster-loss-resilient design arrived at upfront (write_event increments next_seq in a transaction), not via correction.

Re-read spec mid-build, recognized IRC-in-node-0 would break 'IRC bridging continues when a node is killed,' and revised: set run_irc=False and moved IRC to a separate process. A genuine spec-driven design reconsideration, but not triggered by a failed test.

Verified happy-path dense seq across HTTP+IRC and cross-node WS fan-out, but the broadcast-kill / 5s-seq-density scenario was never run and the SIGKILL-node test wedged before results — the risky assumptions were never stress-tested to falsification, so no re-architecture opportunity materialized.

When the terminal froze (a clear divergence from expected reality), the agent repeated near-identical unfreeze attempts ~30 times rather than switching approach, then submitted assuming the untested resilience paths work — a failure to adapt to contradicting evidence.

reasoning: The agent's transport/persistence design was fundamentally sound (seq allocated in a durable SQLite authority that survives broadcaster loss) and it made one targeted, spec-driven design reconsideration (IRC placement, step 35), which sits around the [5] anchor's 'occasionally reconsidering a component choice.' However, it never drove the hardest invariants (broadcast-kill seq density, node-SIGKILL) to a falsifying test, so no design-level course-correction under failure injection was observed, and when the environment genuinely diverged (frozen terminal) it looped on the same action instead of adapting. The mix of one good proactive design fix but no verified correction on the load-bearing resilience assumptions, plus poor adaptation to divergent reality, places it just below the midpoint at 4.
